explanation: Computer systems employ a memory hierarchy to balance cost and performance.  Faster, smaller, and more expensive memory (like caches) sits closer to the CPU, while slower, larger, and cheaper memory (like main memory and disk) is further away.  Caching strategies aim to keep frequently accessed data in faster levels of the hierarchy to improve performance by reducing the average memory access time. Different types of memory (e.g., SRAM, DRAM, Flash) occupy different levels of this hierarchy, each with tradeoffs in speed, cost, and volatility.
syntax: No specific syntax, but concepts include cache levels (L1, L2, L3), cache replacement policies (LRU, FIFO), block size, associativity, and write policies (write-through, write-back).

These technologies occupy different levels in the memory hierarchy.  For instance, SRAM is faster and more expensive, typically used for caches, while DRAM is slower and cheaper, used for main memory. Flash memory represents a non-volatile storage at a lower level of the hierarchy.  The performance of a system is heavily influenced by how effectively the memory hierarchy is utilized, with caching strategies playing a vital role in keeping frequently accessed data readily available in faster memory.
